content: Famotidine is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist that works by inhibiting the production of stomach acid. It is frequently used in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD or GORD). The drug is commonly marketed under the trade names Pepcidine and Pepcid by Johnson & Johnson and Merck. Certain formulations of famotidine are available over the counter (OTC) in various countries. In the United States, 10 mg and 20 mg tablets of famotidine, sometimes combined with a traditional antacid, can be purchased without a prescription. However, higher doses of the medication still require a prescription. Famotidine is also administered to surgical patients prior to operations to prevent post-operative nausea and to reduce the risk of aspiration pneumonitis. Famotidine was developed by Merck & Co. and is marketed through a joint venture between Merck and Johnson & Johnson. During its development, the imidazole ring found in cimetidine was replaced with a 2-guanidinothiazole ring, which resulted in famotidine being 30 times more potent than cimetidine. The drug was first introduced to the market in 1985. In 1999, Pepcid RPD, an orally disintegrating tablet that does not need to be swallowed, was released. Generic versions of famotidine became available in 2001, including products such as Fluxid (Schwarz) and Quamatel (Gedeon Richter Ltd.). In the United States, a product called Pepcid Complete is available, which combines famotidine with an antacid in a chewable tablet to address the relatively slow onset of action of famotidine alone. In the United Kingdom, this combination product is marketed under the name Pepcidtwo.
